items.paragraph: Defenders of reality television often say that nothing in it is scripted, and in a narrow sense they may be right: the participants choose their own words. But a programme is made in the edit as much as on location. Hundreds of hours of footage are cut to a few, and the choice of which glance to keep, which remark to place after which, and what music to lay underneath can turn an ordinary disagreement into a feud or a tired participant into a villain. No line need be invented for a character to be. The question to ask of such shows is therefore not whether they are scripted but how they are assembled, and that is a question their defenders rarely answer.

items.paragraph: Defensive medicine is usually described as a doctor's rational response to the threat of lawsuits: order the extra scan, refer to the specialist, and no court can say you overlooked anything. Many doctors who practise in places where litigation is rare still order tests whose results will not change what they do. What they fear is less a judge than a colleague's raised eyebrow, a patient's disappointment, or their own memory of the one case that went wrong. Reforming malpractice law may therefore reduce unnecessary testing less than its advocates expect. The habit is sustained by a professional culture in which doing more is felt as diligence and doing less as risk, and a culture is not dismantled by a statute.

items.paragraph: Planners in dry regions have often judged land by its average rainfall, asking whether a district receives enough water in a typical year to support crops or herds. The question sounds sensible but can mislead badly. In arid places the average is a statistical fiction that few actual years resemble: runs of meagre seasons are broken by an occasional deluge, and the mean sits between them, describing no year that anyone lives through. Herders who move their animals in search of rain and keep flexible claims to distant pasture are responding to this variability, not ignoring good practice, while schemes that settle them on plots sized for an average year can fail in the first drought. Averages are not useless, since over long periods they still say something about a region's water; but where variation is the dominant fact, a plan built on the mean is a plan for a climate that does not exist.

items.paragraph: Pity and compassion are often treated as the same feeling, but they place the one who feels them differently. Pity looks down. It registers another's misfortune from a position of safety, and it often carries a quiet relief that the misfortune belongs to someone else; this is why people who are pitied so often resent it. It begins from the recognition that the other person's suffering is the kind of thing that could befall anyone, oneself included, and so it treats the sufferer as an equal rather than as an object of concern. The difference is not that one is warmer than the other, for pity can be intensely felt. It is that only compassion leaves the dignity of the sufferer intact.

items.paragraph: A queue is one of the simplest institutions people have invented, and it works with almost no enforcement. items.paragraph: Much of what biologists know about how genes, cells and nervous systems work comes from a small number of species: a fruit fly, a roundworm, a small weed of the mustard family, the laboratory mouse. They were chosen because they breed quickly, survive in captivity and can be manipulated easily, and once a community of researchers had built tools and stocks around them, each new study was cheaper to do in the same species than in a new one. Findings that hold in a mouse may hold in people, and frequently do; but the reasons the mouse was studied had little to do with its resemblance to us.

items.paragraph: When someone collapses on a crowded street, each passer-by is less likely to help than a person who comes upon the same victim alone. This is often read as evidence that crowds make people callous, but the mechanism looks less like indifference than like confusion. In a crowd, everyone checks everyone else's face for cues, and since each person is trying to look calm, the crowd as a whole seems to signal that nothing is wrong. Responsibility is also spread thinly: if many people could act, no one feels that the duty is specifically theirs. Where a single onlooker is singled out, say by being pointed at and asked to call for help, the effect largely disappears.

items.paragraph: Critics of paternalism usually frame the issue as a contest between welfare and freedom: the state may make you better off, but only by overriding your choices. This framing concedes too much to the paternalist and too little to the person. It assumes that we already know what is good for someone independently of what they would choose, so that the only question is whether to impose it. In many cases we do not. Whether a risky career, a strict diet or a dangerous hobby serves a person's welfare depends partly on the plans and commitments that give their life its shape, and these are often visible only in their choices. Respecting someone's decisions is therefore not merely a price paid for liberty; it is frequently our best evidence of what their welfare actually is.

items.paragraph: Abridged editions of classic novels are often defended as a gentle doorway: a twelve-year-old who would abandon an eight-hundred-page original might finish a hundred-page version and come back for the real thing later. What survives is the plot, and plot is the part of a classic that a film or a summary could deliver just as well. items.paragraph: Performing old music on the instruments of its own time has revealed a good deal. Gut strings, valveless horns and lighter keyboards produce textures that modern instruments smooth over, and many listeners have found that familiar works sound clearer and livelier when played this way. Yet the movement's claim to 'authenticity' needs care. items.paragraph: Comparisons of online discussions are often said to show that comment threads in which participants use their real names contain fewer insults than anonymous ones, and the point is regularly offered in support of ending anonymity. The inference moves too fast. Sites that require real names tend to differ from anonymous ones in other ways as well: they are often smaller, more closely moderated and frequented by people who already know one another, any of which could explain the gentler tone. Even where the effect is genuine, it is bought at a price that the comparison does not measure, since the people most likely to fall silent when they must identify themselves include those with the most to fear from speaking, such as an employee criticising an employer. Less abuse in the threads that remain is not the same as better discussion overall.

items.paragraph: Scientists advising the public are often urged to speak with one clear voice, on the theory that any admission of uncertainty will be seized upon and used to justify inaction. The worry is real, but the remedy of projected certainty has a cost that is paid later. When advice delivered as settled turns out to need revision, as advice on a fast-moving problem often does, the public has no way of telling a normal update from an error, and trust falls not only in the revised claim but in the advisers themselves. Stating plainly what is known, what is suspected and what might change does invite some to exploit the gaps. But it also prepares people for revision, so that a change of advice can be read as the system working rather than failing. Candour about uncertainty is not a weakness to be managed; over any length of time it is the condition on which credibility depends.

items.paragraph: Research on smaller classes is often summarised as showing that reducing class size raises achievement, and some carefully designed trials do find gains, especially for younger pupils and those from poorer homes. But the finding is easily stretched. The gains appear when classes shrink substantially and when there are enough capable teachers to staff the new classes; a large programme that must hire quickly may fill many rooms with inexperienced teachers and lose much of the benefit. Smaller classes are also expensive, and the same money might buy other things, such as tutoring or better materials. The evidence supports smaller classes as one useful option under the right conditions, not as a reform that reliably pays off wherever it is tried.

items.paragraph: An old wristwatch that no longer keeps time can be worth almost nothing on the market and still be the last thing a family would sell. Its value lies not in the object's properties, which a replica could match exactly, but in its history: it was on a grandfather's wrist, it was handed over at a particular moment. This is why a perfect copy feels like no substitute. Heirlooms work as anchors for memories that would otherwise have nothing to attach to, and they make the past something one can hold. The same feature, however, makes them a burden when the history they carry is one the inheritors would rather forget.
